# Nonlinearities and interactions {#sec-nonlinearity} The feature work so far asked *which* information helps. This chapter asks *how* it helps: which relationships are curved, which have thresholds, and which variables interact. Those answers are what feature engineering should target. There are two lenses: 1. **What did the model learn?** SHAP values [@lundberg_shap] on the points model. 2. **Where is the market wrong?** Segments where the closing line misses systematically. ## First, a direct test: do interactions help at all? An additive model can't represent interactions: gradient boosting with single-split trees (stumps) builds $f(x) = \sum_j f_j(x_j)$. If deeper trees, which *can* learn interactions, don't beat stumps, the data holds no interactions a model can exploit. In every experiment (@tbl-additive, copied from the experiment logs), the additive model matched or beat the deeper ones: | Feature set | Additive (stumps) | Depth 2 | 15 leaves | |---|---|---|---| | v1 (scores only) | 9.460 | 9.482 | 9.607 | | v2 (+ CFBD efficiency, priors) | 9.295 | 9.302 | 9.419 | : Walk-forward CV MAE: additive vs interaction-capable LightGBM. {#tbl-additive} ## Model lens: shapes of the main effects The model below is deliberately deeper than the tuned one (15 leaves), so interactions *can* show up if they exist. ::: {#cell-fig-shap-shapes .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Mean SHAP value by feature decile: points the model adds to the ratings' prediction.](nonlinearity_files/figure-html/fig-shap-shapes-output-1.svg){#fig-shap-shapes} ::: ::: | Feature | Shape | Reading | Feature idea | |---|---|---|---| | Expected game total | +2 → −2 points, steepest at the ends | Ratings overstate high-scoring games: **regression to the mean** | Shrink extremes; a **shootout** flag | | Talent difference | Negative tail, flat middle, positive tail | Only **big** talent gaps matter | Tail/threshold features | | Returning production | Strongly negative in the lowest decile, flat above the median | Heavy roster turnover hurts | Low-returning-production threshold | | Expected success rate | Convex, largest at the top | Elite efficiency carries information that points miss | Elite-efficiency tail | ## Model lens: interaction strength ::: {#tbl-interactions .cell tbl-cap='Strongest pairwise SHAP interactions (mean absolute contribution, points).' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

The market is more accurate than the model on average, but it might still be wrong in particular *places*. Every candidate feature was cut into quintiles (on 2016–2023), and each segment's over rate (vs the closing total) or home-cover rate (vs the closing spread) was tested. Then the same segments were checked on **2024–2025**, which was never used to find them. ::: {#tbl-market-lens .cell tbl-cap='Segments where the closing line missed in 2016–2023 (|z| ≥ 2), with the 2024–25 holdout.' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

Two patterns: - **Totals: every surviving segment points the same way, and it holds in the holdout.** High expected totals, high closing totals and very fast pace all lean **under**. - **Spreads: the "significant" segments flip sign in the holdout.** That's noise from testing many bins. {{< pagebreak >}} ## The shootout-under effect Define a **shootout** as a game where the ratings' expected total is in the top 20% (above 63\.5 points, a threshold set on 2016–2023). ::: {#cell-fig-shootout .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Under rate vs the closing total: expected shootouts vs all games, by season. Dashed line: 52.4% break-even at −110.](nonlinearity_files/figure-html/fig-shootout-output-1.svg){#fig-shootout} ::: ::: - **Every season from 2021 to 2025** went 55–60% under in expected shootouts (2019: 59.9%; 2020, the COVID season: 51.7%; 2015–2018 near 50%). - The gap is there **even in over-heavy years**: in 2024 only 48% of all games went under, but 55% of expected shootouts did. - **Against the bettable opening total**, 2021–2025 pooled: 56\.4% under on 509 games, above break-even in each of the five seasons. It's the same nonlinearity as the expected-total SHAP curve, seen from the market side: **games that look like shootouts get overestimated, by the ratings and by the market.** It became paper rule B (@sec-betting). An honest caveat: the 20% cut was chosen while looking at 2016–2023, which includes 2021–2023; the clean confirmation is 2024–2025. ## From insights to a totals model (issue #10) The natural next step was to feed every insight into a dedicated totals model: explicit nonlinear terms (shootout flag, squared distance from an average total, high-line flag, pace tail, talent-gap tail, low returning production, early season, blowout game script, and gap × shootout), trained on the under vs the closing total and graded vs the opener. Results are copied from `notebooks/03_total/full_game.ipynb`: | Model | Log loss (close, 2019–23) | Win % vs open, 2021–23 | Win % vs open, 2024–25 | |---|---|---|---| | Logistic, base features | 0.693 | 55.3 (870) | 50.5 (475) | | Logistic, + nonlinear terms | 0.694 | 52.7 (1,025) | 50.0 (608) | | LightGBM additive, + nonlinear | 0.693 | 53.5 (609) | 44.6 (233) | | LightGBM depth 3, + nonlinear | 0.696 | 53.5 (1,106) | 50.7 (671) | | **Rule B: under if expected total > 63.5** | — | **56.6 (355)** | **56.4 (156)** | | Always under | 0.693 | 51.8 | 51.7 | : Totals model vs the one-line rule. Coin-flip log loss is 0.693; break-even is 52.4%. {#tbl-totals} **The lesson:** the insight is real, but flexible models overfit it. None beats a coin flip against the close, and the 2021–23 gains vanish in 2024–25. The single threshold captures the effect and holds. One more finding: totals drift *down* from open to close on average, so "always under" collects positive CLV; rule B's CLV is at or below that drift, so the market doesn't move toward its picks. Either it's a persistent inefficiency or luck, and only live results can tell. **The A-vs-B conflict, resolved with data** (out-of-sample 2021–2025): rule A's *overs* in expected shootouts won 48.5% (99 bets), its unders there 57.6% (66). In the 99 games where A said over and B said under, the under won 51.5%, so neither side pays. **Conflicts are skipped**, and the weekly summary reports a "portfolio" line (A + B, no bet when they disagree) next to each rule's own record.
